notes.title: Space Marmalade Dev Log 2
notes.notes:
Hi all,

What follows is a documentation of my design and solutions to creating a procedural universe system for Space Marmalade. I hope it'll be of interest to any following development of the game. This technique can be broken into 3 parts. 

[olist]
[*] Randomish Seeding
[*] L-Systems (kinda)
[*] Planitification 
[/olist]

This gives us a pretty planetoid visualiser, which I plan to translate into a space exploration system.
(For the purposes of this article, I'll be referring to "Stars", "Planets", "Moons", etc as Planetoids to save from repeating)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40422943/9bb4f239b88e82340b0eede1c061c9703e1f2b3d.gif[/img]

[h2]1. Randomish Seeding[/h2]

An essential component in Space Marmalade for me, is a [i]deterministic procedural generation[/i] tied into the character creation system. That is to say, "if someone creates the same spaceship, that spaceship should be in the same 'universe'." To me, this is a solution to the "Inattentional blindness" problem that rogue-like games develop over time. In these games, [i]because[/i] the game is different every time, the differences begin to feel less and less significant to the player as they grow accustomed to the formula that generates these worlds. The player is rarely given time to properly familiarize and develop an attachment to a procedural level, and once left it can become lost forever.

Instead, we can hash the choices a player makes when creating a ship into a seed value. Since these choices are largely aesthetical and difficulty selections, this creates a lot of personal significance and depth to making a seed. As the player builds an understanding for that solar systems "map", they can also share the combination of ship selections to another player and collaborate their exploration.


[h2]2. L Systems (kinda)[/h2]

Once a seed has been determined, we can store this value in a string. My concept is to build an L-system that could convert strings into a solar system-like structure. When designing the system, I took inspiration from existing file path systems (eg: User/Documents/text.txt).  I can use the "depth" of the path to determine the type of planetoid in the system (eg: the path Seed/Galaxy/Planet/Moon is a Moon). 

One advantage of this pathing approach is that it is easy to traverse, by simply adding and removing '/'s. Another advantage is that saving the players position in this structure is as simple as recording a string. 


[h2]3. Planetification[/h2]

Once we have a path to the planetoid we want, we can hash this value to give us a deterministic random number. Using this value, we can determine the colour, size, and sprites of the planet. By removing the planetoids name at the end of the path, we can visualise the "parent" of the planetoid.  We can also calculate the number of "children" the planetoid has, append their names to the path, and visualise those planetoids.


This approach allows us to explore a near-infinite star system with a small amount of computing and without any costly memory overhead. 

I hope as the game nears completion, the advantages of this system will become more and more apparent.

Thanks for reading! 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/40422943/7e868e8566f25231a34f6978651c459fc151b5fc.png[/img]

notes.title: Space Marmalade Dev Log 1
notes.notes:
It has been a busy year! During the year of lockdown,  I finished University, got my first job and moved out of the home. 

I am a game developer. I've worked on several game projects, having published at least one mobile game.  I work full time as a programmer. This means I've got a pretty solid set of game development skills and experience to back me on my gamedev journey! 

I want to document my development as I go, to motivate myself and to keep players in the loop with how the game is progressing. Maybe it will also be insightful to other Indie developers?

With all that in mind... Why is making a game hard?

As I write this, I am reminded of a quote I picked up when vising a games exhibition at the  V&A museum.

"Making games combines everything that's hard about building a bridge with everything hard about composing an opera. Games are operas made out of bridges." 
- Frank Lantz, 2014

The first thing to unpack is bridges. Like an incomplete bridge, an unfinished game is not really useful to a user (except as an example of what not to do).

Second, operas need an orchestra. This is relevant to games because making games requires many specialized skills. Programming, art, audio... These don't even begin to scratch project management and marketing. You can't play all the instruments at once, you need a band.

Third thing is, balancing the product for the opera-listener and the bridge-walker. A game has to be fun and engaging, while also being tidy and functional.  These are not exclusive concepts, but the exact balance will differ from user to user.  No matter how perfect, there will always be room for improvement. 

In short, the three "rules" for difficulty-free game development are:
1. Have attainable goals. 
2. Don't work alone, have a team.
3. Be open to player criticism.

It's no surprise that game jam teams who embrace these concepts can produce amazing work.

So, how does Space Marmalade measure up?

1. Space Marmalade has been making steady progress, trying to hit milestones for each 
 #ScreenshotSaturday to generate interest in the game
2. We do have a team at the moment. I'm thrilled at the prospect of working with 
veterans Chase Bethea (Game Music Composer) and Manovermars (Artist).
3. Space Marmalade is still very early in development. It has a few video clips, a gamejam submission, and a discord to offer feedback on. Additionally, this blog might become a new avenue for feedback.

---

When I started this blog entry, I sent an initial draft to my girlfriend and close friends. 
The feedback I got back was, it was far too negative! I glossed over a lot of my accomplishments, 
focusing on what the game didn't have. 

It was definitely cathartic to get a lot of the worries on my mind on paper. 
Yet when I read back, I realized what I had written was very from the actual truth 
(which is why it should now read much nicer!).
 
I was feeling an aversion to my game, not because I stopped enjoying it, but because of feeling constant stress. I'd put this stress on myself, wanting the best for my game.

To me, the hardest part of game development is therefore in the Mind. We want our games to be good. We put a lot of thought into what the game needs to be good,  and when we should be there. When we fall short, it's easy to fall into a cycle of analyzing why.  "Am I not working hard enough?", "Have I not been passionate enough?", "Is there something more I can do?"

Burnout is actually very common in our industry, and I suspect this probably connects to how long games take to finish. I can draw a piece of art in a day, put down the pen, and think "I'm happy with that" or "I'm not happy with that". 

I would struggle to work on the same piece of art for over a year in the same way. 

In a way, keeping this log forces me to confront myself and my feelings, which is a good thing. This challenges me to learn to be honest with myself, rather than pressing on regardless. 

I hope as I continue working on Space Marmalade, I'll be able to share the lessons I learn along the way!
